newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA OPTION VOLS EDGE HIGHER AHEAD OF FX MOVES.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA OPTION VOLS EDGE HIGHER AHEAD OF FX MOVES.

text.p: Uncertainty about events post-July 1 have led to increased demand for short-term rand option volatilities as players long of rand and bonds hedge themselves ahead of the relaxation of exchange controls.

As local banks position themselves for the expected demand for foreign currency around that time, dealers say there is a risk of stop losses which have accumulated at just above the 4.50 level being triggered.

From July 1, South African individuals will be allowed to invest offshore or hold foreign currency bank accounts for the first time, although the amount of capital they will be allowed to export has yet to be announced.

Traders say that the concerns that the exchange control relaxations will result in capital flight has led both local and offshore players currently long domestic bonds and currency to hedge themselves in the options market.
Dealers said that implied rand option volatilities in the two and three month areas had edged up to between 6.0 to 6.75 and 7.0 to 8.0 respectively from 5.5/6.5 and 6.75/7.75 recently.
"The vols have edged up marginally which is an indication that people are nervous about July 1," an options trader said.
"There is demand for out-of-the-money rand puts in the two and three months just as a hedge," another trader added.
"A lot of people who are sitting long bonds and rand are hedging themselves over the July 1 date just in case," another options trader added.

Dealers said that while there was growing consensus in the market that the exchange control steps were likely to be a non-event, there was a risk that the rand could weaken sharply as banks buy more foreign currency to meet expected demand from residents.

"If we are going to see big demand for foreign currency from the man in the street to invest money offshore there could be fairly big demand for foreign currency post July 1," a senior forex trader said.
"That could trigger stop losses which have been building up at around 4.5050 to 4.51," he added.
Dealers said the 4.5050 to 4.51 area represented an important support line for the rand, which if pierced, could signal a rapid move to around 4.55.
"But that in itself would not be a bad thing because it will square the market out," the trader said.
Given the current offshore appetite for rands, he added a shake-out would probably be brief as foreigners looked to come back into the market by going long rand again.
